newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Khmer Rouge dissidents to join Cambodian armed forces.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge dissidents to join Cambodian armed forces.

text.p: Breakaway Khmer Rouge commanders have agreed to merge their force of up to 4,000 fighters with Cambodian government forces on November 6, top officials from both sides said on Sunday.
The decision came as the Khmer Rouge suffered thousands of defectors over the weekend, including several thousand fighters from fronts located close to the bases of the breakaway rebels.
The fighters, from front 250 in the northwest and 909 in the southwest, included Sam Bit, said to be second in line to dissident Khmer Rouge leader Ieng Sary.
Sok Peap, commander of the northwest base of Phnom Malai, told Reuters that Ieng Sary had decided to integrate his estimated 4,000 fighters with the Royal Cambodian Armed Forces.

Ek Sereywath, secretary of state for defence, told Reuters that armed forces deputy chief of staff General Nhiek Bun Chhay had flown to Ieng Sary's Pailin stronghold in the northwest to finalise preparations for Wednesday's ceremony.

In a statement read on local radio, soldiers from front 250, which includes four divisions and one regiment, said their 3,400 fighters and 25,000 family members were ready to defect to the government. The statement was dated November 1.
Senior commanders of front 250 and front 909 told a news conference in Phnom Penh on Sunday they were not prepared to wait any longer for Ieng Sary when they lacked food and medicine.
The announcements speed the unravelling of the Khmer Rouge hardliners since early August, when Ieng Sary broke with forces loyal to Khmer Rouge supremo Pol Pot.
Ieng Sary was pardoned in September for his role in the brutal Khmer Rouge regime of 1975-1979 that left more than one million Cambodians dead from murder, overwork, disease and malnutrition.
The royal amnesty from a 1979 death sentence allowed peace talks to resume between the government and his guerrillas.

Co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen last month met separately with Ieng Sary in Pailin, and their independent negotiations have led to a widening rift within the coalition government that shows no signs of mending soon, analysts said.
Ranariddh said on Saturday he brought Sok Peap and Ei Chien, commander of Pailin, to Phnom Penh last week for talks about tensions between rival guerrillas and integration with the army.
Ranariddh said he believed the breakaway fighters deserved at least one general staff position, a proposal Hun Sen has rejected.
Hun Sen, in his radio speech on Sunday, blamed the delays in Ieng Sary's merger on unnamed politicians in Phnom Penh.

"Our country is very sorry and our compatriots are very sad because some politicians in Phnom Penh tell the breakaway Khmer Rouge to demand top positions," he said. "This case makes the Cambodian people fall into bloodshed again."
